Description.value: Browser Use is an open-source Python library (MIT) that makes websites accessible to AI agents. It connects large language models to a Chromium browser via CDP, extracting the DOM and screenshots on each step, then executing LLM-decided actions until the task is complete. Available as a pip package, a CLI tool, and a managed cloud API.

evidence.quote: Make websites accessible for AI agents.

The Agent class is the unit of work. You pass it a task, an LLM, and a BrowserSession. On each step it takes a screenshot and extracts the DOM in parallel, sends both to the LLM to decide the next action, executes that action, and repeats until the task is done.

Practices.Summary: An automated end-to-end evaluation pipeline runs 100 web agent tasks in parallel in under 5 minutes on every PR, using Blacksmith runners on GitHub Actions. Evaluation tasks are drawn from millions of real LLM-labeled user spans rather than synthetic environments, ensuring coverage of real-world page complexity.

evidence.quote: Using Blacksmith runners on GitHub Actions, we achieve insane scaling, running 100 complex web tasks in parallel in under 5 minutes end-to-end.

We sourced our evaluation tasks from millions of LLM-labeled user spans rather than synthetic sites, because synthetic environments completely fail to capture the bizarre reality, complexity, and ugliness of how the actual web is built.

We built the LLM judge directly into the agent code itself, running after the agent returns done. This means that the judge can also double as a real-time validation layer for the agent during regular use.
This pipeline isn't just for manual testing—it runs automatically on every single PR in our open-source repo to guarantee we don't regress performance.

Practices.Summary: Statistical rigor is applied to evaluation: each task is run multiple times and results are aggregated with statistical bootstrapping, because single-run deterministic tests are unsuitable for non-deterministic web agents.

evidence.quote: You need real statistical rigor. That means running the exact same task multiple times, messing with a ton of agentic settings, ensuring perfect reproducibility of those settings, and aggregating the results with statistical bootstrapping.
It's concerning that many AI agent benchmarks do not include error bars or variance estimations; coming from backgrounds in experimental particle physics, that lack of statistical rigor is alarming.

Practices.Summary: The cloud production architecture uses an SQS-to-Lambda pattern: a FastAPI service (ECS Fargate) accepts task requests, writes a database row, drops an SQS message, and returns HTTP 202 in under 50 ms. A Lambda worker pulls each message and runs the agent to completion.

evidence.quote: The handler validates the payload, creates session and task rows in the database, commits, sends an SQS message, and returns HTTP 202 with the task ID in under 50 milliseconds. The work hasn't started yet.
The API is a FastAPI service on ECS Fargate. Behind it is a standard SQS queue with one message per agent run carrying the task ID and execution config.

Practices.Summary: Lambda's 15-minute hard limit is handled by a continuation mechanism: 2 minutes before the deadline, the agent checkpoints its state to S3, sends a new SQS message with an incremented counter, and a fresh Lambda invocation restores and resumes the session. Continuations are capped at 12 (~3 hours wall-clock).

evidence.quote: Two minutes before the Lambda deadline, the agent stops gracefully... The handler checkpoints state to S3, sends a new SQS message with the continuation counter incremented, and returns success. A new Lambda invocation picks up that message, fetches the state from S3, restores the Agent, and resumes from the last completed step.

Practices.Summary: The same container image runs across local development, evaluation pipelines, and production. A single config switch (sandbox_mode: 'docker' | 'ukc') determines whether the image runs as a Docker container or a Unikraft micro-VM.

evidence.quote: Pattern 1: Single backend with agent loop and isolated terminal use sandbox; Pattern 2: Isolate the agent. The entire agent runs in a sandbox with zero secrets. It talks to the outside world through a control plane that holds all the credentials. The agent becomes disposable. No secrets to steal, no state to preserve, you can kill it, restart it, scale it independently. The control plane holds the truth..

The agent becomes disposable. No secrets to steal, no state to preserve, you can kill it, restart it, scale it independently. The control plane holds the truth. A single config switch (sandbox_mode: 'docker' | 'ukc') controls which path the code takes. We went with Pattern 2. The control plane holds all credentials and acts as a proxy for everything: LLM calls, file storage, billing. The sandbox receives three env variables and has no access to anything else. It runs as a Unikraft micro-VM in production and a Docker container in development and evals. Same image everywhere.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: asyncio.gather without return_exceptions=True in _get_ax_tree_for_all_frames causes total DOM extraction failure
Issues.Description: Missing return_exceptions=True in an asyncio.gather call meant any single failing frame silently cancelled all other DOM extraction tasks, causing complete accessibility-tree failures. Reveals systemic gaps in async error propagation discipline.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: when using LMStudio nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-4b agent prints invalid json error
Issues.Description: LLM output from a locally-served model was not valid JSON, crashing the action-parsing loop with no graceful fallback. Exposes insufficient LLM output validation for non-standard model providers.

Issues.Issue_Title: [Bug] AttributeError: items when using Custom OpenAI/DeepSeek models (Pydantic ConfigDict clash)
Issues.Description: A Pydantic v2 ConfigDict conflict between browser-use's base model class and the LangChain wrapper for custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints caused an AttributeError at runtime. Highlights brittle model-compatibility handling across third-party LLM providers.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: list_chrome_profiles local_state Missing encoding parameter causes garbled output on non-ASCII systems
Issues.Description: Omitting an explicit encoding parameter when reading Chrome's local_state JSON file produced mojibake on non-UTF-8 system locales (e.g., Simplified Chinese). Indicates a systemic lack of explicit encoding handling in file I/O code paths.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: upload_image does not fail on file max limit
Issues.Description: The upload_image action silently accepted files exceeding the maximum allowed size instead of raising an error, allowing oversized payloads to reach downstream APIs. Points to missing input boundary validation in file-handling actions.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: upload_image should fail but passes when file does not meet validation criteria
Issues.Description: Companion to #4670 — validation logic for uploaded images was either absent or not enforced, allowing invalid files to pass through without error. Reveals a gap in systematic input validation testing for action primitives.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: mac install fails with RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread 'MainThread'.
Issues.Description: On macOS, calling asyncio APIs without an existing event loop in the main thread raised an unhandled RuntimeError at startup. Highlights async event-loop lifecycle mismanagement as a cross-platform compatibility risk.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: Pagination classifier mislabels first/last controls as prev/next when using shared symbols («, »)
Issues.Description: The pagination-detection heuristic confused «/» glyphs (used as both first/last and previous/next in different designs) causing incorrect navigation. Exposes fragile symbol-based UI classification in the DOM-parsing layer.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: sensitive_data redaction breaks when one secret is substring of another (partial leak)
Issues.Description: When two secrets shared a substring relationship the shorter secret was masked first, leaving the longer one partially visible in LLM context and logs. A security-critical bug: partial credential leaks into prompt history.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: Windows: --profile fails with WinError 32 when Chrome is running (profile copy vs file locks)
Issues.Description: On Windows, attempting to copy a Chrome profile directory while Chrome held file locks caused a WinError 32 crash. Demonstrates platform-specific filesystem-locking assumptions not accounted for in the profile management code.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: close --all leaves daemon and temp-profile Chrome processes running
Issues.Description: The 'close --all' CLI command did not terminate background daemon and temporary Chrome profile processes, causing resource leaks on the host machine. Part of a pattern of incomplete process lifecycle management.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: action field returned as JSON string instead of list when done-text contains newlines (Claude Sonnet)
Issues.Description: When Claude Sonnet's done-action text contained newline characters the action field was serialized as a raw JSON string rather than a parsed list, breaking the action dispatcher. Reveals LLM-provider-specific output schema fragility.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: browser-use close does not terminate daemon and Chrome processes
Issues.Description: The base 'close' command also failed to fully shut down daemon and browser processes, leaving orphaned processes consuming system resources. Precursor to #4539 — same root pattern of incomplete subprocess teardown.

Issues.Issue_Title: browser-use fails to identify/click icon-only 'Create Test' button when tooltip is present but accessible label is missing
Issues.Description: The DOM interaction layer relied on accessible labels rather than visual/tooltip context, causing the agent to skip buttons that have tooltips but no ARIA label. Reveals a systemic gap in the accessibility-tree-based element detection strategy.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: Azure OpenAI false content_filter / ResponsibleAIPolicyViolation (jailbreak detected) on normal navigation/login prompts
Issues.Description: Azure OpenAI's content safety layer incorrectly flagged standard browser-use navigation and login prompts as jailbreak attempts, blocking normal agent operation. Highlights the lack of provider-specific prompt hardening or safety-filter bypass strategies.

Others.Summary: A concurrent credits billing race condition was fixed by replacing asyncio.Lock (process-scoped, ineffective across pods) with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (database-level row locking). An earlier clever fix had already caused a different problem at scale by locking the same user row exclusively under high load.

evidence.quote: Credit deduction used asyncio.Lock keyed by user ID in a Python dictionary. Works on one process but does nothing across pods. Concurrent requests on different pods could double-spend credits without either process knowing. Replaced it with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which is what I should have used from the start.

Others.Summary: Memory leak from non-singleton HTTP clients required seven commits in one day to fully resolve. ssl.create_default_context() was found to take ~1.8s of CPU per call, blocking the event loop under load.

evidence.quote: Every LLM call was creating a new httpx client and each one allocates a connection pool that never closes... ssl.create_default_context() takes ~1.8s of CPU, so per-request client creation was blocking the event loop under load. An entire day to learn that HTTP clients should be singletons.

Practices.Summary: Browser Use adopts a minimal-agent philosophy: 'An agent is just a for-loop of messages. Give the LLM as much freedom as possible, then vibe-restrict based on evals' The original first agent was discarded and rebuilt from scratch after the team reverse-engineered Claude Code and Gemini CLI. They discovered that fewer abstractions produce more reliable agents, because LLM can learn from mistakes by reasoning.

evidence.quote: Agent frameworks fail not because models are weak, but because their action spaces are incomplete. Instead of defining every possible action up front, start from the opposite assumption: the model can do almost anything. Then restrict. Give the LLM as much freedom as possible, then vibe-restrict based on evals.
The bitter lesson: The less you build, the more it works.

Practices.Summary: An 'inversion' principle guides feature design: start from maximal capability (expose raw CDP to the model), then restrict based on evaluation data rather than pre-defining a fixed action space. This allows the system to scale with improved models instead of fighting them.

evidence.quote: Instead of defining every possible action up front, start from the opposite assumption: the model can do almost anything. Then restrict. Give the LLM as much freedom as possible, then vibe-restrict based on evals.
That's what lets the system scale with better models instead of fighting them.  Don't over-specify intelligence - let the model reason

Practices.Summary: The team moved from Playwright to raw CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol) to eliminate a second network hop (Node.js relay server) and gain direct control over tab crash handling, cross-origin iframe routing, and browser events. A new event-driven watchdog architecture was introduced to respond to CDP events asynchronously.

evidence.quote: By switching to raw CDP we've massively increased the speed of element extraction, screenshots, and all our default actions.
Playwright also introduces a 2nd network hop going through a node.js playwright server websocket, which incurs a meaningful amount of latency when we do thousands of CDP calls.

Practices.Summary: Fast iteration with systematic learning: the cloud infrastructure was built through 4,000+ commits in one year. Mistakes were shipped, analyzed, and fixed forward. The gap between a working demo and production reliability defined the team's engineering maturity curve.

evidence.quote: The gap between 'works in a demo' and 'works at scale' is about 4,000 commits. This is what most of them looked like.
You mess up, you learn, you mess up again, you learn again. The loop never stops, but you get faster at the learning part.
